Thank you, Mr. Speaker. At this juncture I rose to protest the statement made by the Prime Minister. I said that statement was not only inaccurate but was not in accordance with the fact. The Prime Minister replied that I would have an opportunity to say so at a future date if I felt like doing so. That is exactly what I intend to do now. The Prime Minister, however, went on and said this, as reported at page 64 of Hansard:
I am saying they did not do anything effective during those years. They did one thing. They talked about inflation. They cried over it. During the period between 1945 and 1957, freight rates increased by 120 per cent.
Then later, as found on the same page, he said:
We find ourselves, by horizontal increases, placed in an ever more difficult position. The Leader of the Opposition says "Why do they not act?" For 12 years the increases went on and the government of which he was a member did nothing.

Sir, that is not so. That statement is not only inaccurate but is unfounded in fact, as I intend to prove. Let me pause here for a moment to say this. When the Prime Minister came in the house, as he did the other evening, and invited the house to give suggestions with reference to the establishment of a royal commission and the scope of that commission and spoke calmly and coolly, let me say to him that I prefer that attitude on his part rather than the political attitude which was adopted not only in this statement which he made but when he and others say "Oh, you have been here for 22 years but you have done absolutely nothing". In so far as freight rates are concerned I say that the former government has an excellent record of which it can boast.
But the Prime Minister was not alone in making that statement. The Ottawa Journal which is a fairly close follower of the Prime Minister and his friends, published an editorial following the statement made by the Prime Minister on December 1, 1958. I should like to read part of this editorial into the record. It is entitled "Mr. Pearson and Railways" and it reads in part as follows:
Mr. Pearson opposes a freight increase for the railways, says they should have been given a subsidy instead, charges that the government allowed the railway problem to "drift".
What did the government of which Mr. Pearson was a member allow the railway problem to do?
In 1948, ten years ago, the government announced with a blare of trumpets that it had asked the board of railway commissioners to look into the whole railway rate structure, to look especially into geographical rate inequities.
It has been a long look; and during that whole decade of looking Canada experienced one crippling railway strike, plus almost continuous dispute over railway rates and wages. It is not on record that Mr. Pearson or any of his colleagues ever did anything to hurry along the job they had given to the board of railway commissioners or did anything else whatever about railway rate inequities.
That editorial is as inaccurate, unfounded and unwarranted as is the statement which the Prime Minister has made.
Let us now look at the facts, Mr. Speaker, and let us consider the applications that were made to the board of transport commissioners over the years. The first general increase in freight rates came in 1917, and I need not remind the house what government was in office at that time. That increase amounted to 15 per cent. The second increase came in 1918, one year later, and it amounted to 25 per cent. I need not tell the house who was in office then, because the house knows. But do you know how it was done, Mr. Speaker? It was done not by way of application to the board of transport commissioners but by an order from the cabinet to the board of transport commissioners to increase the freight

Freight Rates
rates by 25 per cent. That was the way in which a Conservative administration proceeded to deal with freight rates in those years. Then in 1920, still under a Conservative administration, there was an increase of 40 per cent, following an application at this time by the Railway Association of Canada to the board.
Then in 1921, when a Liberal administration took office, the 40 per cent increase was reduced, first by 5 per cent in 1921, then by 10 per cent in the same year and that reduction was followed by a further reduction in August of 1922, leaving the effect of the 40 per cent increase as follows: 17J per cent in eastern Canada and 12J per cent in western Canada.
So much for what was done under a Conservative administration with reference to freight rates. I insist on putting this on the record for the simple purpose of telling those of our friends who sit on the other side of the house that we on this side are getting tired, as I am sure the people of Canada are, of the government's practice, every time something happens in this country, by which they delight in telling us, "Oh, this is what you did when you were in office". It is about time the government stood on its own feet and made decisions without always saying "Oh, this is what you did when you were in office". We have been having that practice followed for some time. We had it followed by the Minister of Finance this afternoon. We had it followed by the Prime Minister with reference to the immigration order when it was before the house yesterday. Can we not have decisions, announcements and statements by the government without always having a reference made to the fact that this was done by the former administration, and that the government either was carrying on those policies or even making them better? Surely the time has come now that they have been in office for 20 months, almost two years, when they should be able to make decisions of their own and give the reasons for them.
It has been intimated by the statements and the editorial in the Journal that when we on this side of the house were the Liberal administration we had done nothing with reference to the question of rates. Listen to this. In 1897-

Very well, I will come right down to 1957 if my hon. friends will bear with me; but do not forget that the statement was broad, just as all these statements are from the other side of the house. It is said, either through the Prime Minister or through this editorial, that we were in office for 22 years

and did nothing, so may I be allowed to say what we did. I say that the lowest freight rates ever put into effect in this country were the Crowsnest rates which were established under the Laurier regime in 1897. Then in 1903 the Liberal government enacted the Railway Act which authorized the establishment of the board of transport commissioners, the board which deals with these matters. That is the very board, Mr. Speaker, which our friends on the other side of the house want to destroy and see disappear, and I will be able to prove in an instant that a motion was made to that effect by hon. members opposite when they sat on this side of the house.
Then in 1924 the Liberal government inaugurated an investigation to determine whether it was possible to equalize freight rates in Canada, and it was found that it was possible. In 1927 the Liberal government introduced the Maritime Freight Rates Act, giving the benefit of a 20 per cent reduction in freight rates to the select maritime area. From 1948 to 1950 it reduced and then removed the mountain differential. It reduced the mountain differential first from l j miles on the prairies equalling 1 mile on the Pacific coast, to 1J miles, and then reduced the 1J miles to 1 mile, removing the mountain differential entirely in 1950. The mountain differential was a matter of great contention over the years, and I submit that is something which well might be given consideration.
But the greater part of the criticism levelled at the Liberal administration was with reference to P.C. 1487. That was an order in council under which the board of transport commissioners were authorized to make a thorough study of the rate structure of the railway companies with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which would, under substantially the same conditions and circumstances, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and the extension of Canadian trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of agricultural and other basic commodities.
The Prime Minister, sir, ridiculed that investigation. I have in my hand the three reports which the board of transport commissioners handed down under this investigation, and I would like to refer briefly to them. The first report was made on March 25, 1955, and the effect of this first report was to substantially reduce class rates in western Canada to equalize these class rates, a matter which the provinces had been asking for over the years. I wonder if the Prime Minister

or his followers have read or studied this interim report on the equalization of freight rates, because it is well worth reading.
The second report under the investigation I have referred to was brought down on September 23, 1957, and I would just like to read one short paragraph from it. It states that-
-the first phase of equalization throughout Canada, namely, of class rates accompanied by a new freight rate classification, had been accomplished and made effective on March 1st, 1955.
Later, on page 4, it is stated:
The equalized class rates have now been in effect for two and one-half years and have cured the complaints that existed for so many years concerning the higher class rates in western Canada compared with eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
How
could that principle possibly have been established when at the same time the railways were allowed to set competitive rates? I am not saying that they should not have been allowed to do that; obviously they had to. But where there was competition in one area and not in another, how could the freight rates possibly have become equalized?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend must make a distinction between class and commodity rates and competitive rates. This judgment does not deal, as my hon. friend knows, with competitive rates, because the competitive rates have always been excluded by the railways in their applications to the board of transport commissioners, and the reference to the board dealt with exactly the same subject matter that is being dealt with now by the minister in the subsidy of $20 million. I did not deal with competitive rates, because competitive rates are determined by other forms of transportation such as motor vehicles or water carriers. I think that is why this equalization dealt only with other than the exceptions mentioned in the order in council.
The Prime Minister complained about the tremendous length of time it took for the board to deal with this equalization under P.C. 1487. Well, the judgment of the board as recorded on page 4-the final judgment dated December 22, 1958-states that it was not possible to proceed with the equalization of these rates until January, 1952, and gives the reason therefor. It then goes on-and this will be of interest, I am sure, to the hon. member who interrupted me-to give the number of judgments which the board had handed down in order to equalize freight rates, and there are 13 of these judgments, beginning on January 10, 1952 and ending on January 19, 1958. Hon. members will find on page 5 a detailed statement concerning many of the class and commodity rates which have been equalized.
Thus I say this, in so far as the report, the investigation and the study under P.C. 1487 are concerned; that the board did a commendable job and the Prime Minister, instead of criticizing the board, should be commending it. The Prime Minister said it took a long time. Well, in the United States it took 12 years to enable freight rates to be equalized, so even if it has taken Canada seven years-and the job is still not done-I do not think we should be too surprised.

Freight Rates
Now I come to 1948, when the government of the day established a royal commission on transportation, the Turgeon commission. That commission produced the most exhaustive study ever made in this country of the problem we are now discussing. The Prime Minister, when he was on this side of the house, welcomed the announcement of the royal commission and spoke approvingly of it. The work of this commission was expeditiously handled; but let me point out to the minister that notwithstanding the fact that the commission was appointed on December 28, 1948 it did not issue its report until February 9, 1951, more than two years later.
So I say to him with deference that if the royal commission which he and the government intend to set up is going to do the kind of job the government expects it will do, it should be encouraged to carry out a thorough investigation, and it should not be limited with regard to time in such a way it has been limited both by the Prime Minister's statement and by the minister's own announcement.
Finally, in 1951 the then government of Canada accepted the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation. It accepted all the recommendations having to do with freight rates and many other recommendations incidental thereto, and these were brought into this house, implemented by way of legislation and put into effect. It was stated at that time in this house that this was the most important and forward looking piece of legislation having to do with freight rates ever introduced in Canada. Notwithstanding that statement there are still accusations from the other side that nothing was done.
Let me go into detail with reference to What was done by the previous administration by way of implementing the recommendations of the Turgeon commission. First of all we brought in legislation which provided for the payment of a subsidy of $7 million for the maintenance of the trackage through northern Ontario which serves as a link or bridge between certain points in that part of the province of Ontario. That is the matter which the Prime Minister said was the only thing done of any consequence.
Let us see what other things done were of consequence. Legislation next provided for the establishment of a national freight rate policy as enacted in section 336 of the Railway Act. This was an over-all direction to the board by a section which stated that every railway company shall so far as reasonably possible in respect of all freight traffic of the same description and carried on or upon a like kind of car, passing over all lines or routes of the company in Canada,

charge tolls to all persons at the same rate whether by weight, mileage or otherwise, with the exceptions mentioned in subsection 4 of section 336. This is what the board of transport commissioners tried to do. Using P.C.1487, as I have said, in conjunction with this amendment, section 336 of the Railway Act, the board tried, and succeeded in large measure, to equalize freight rates.
This section was, I submit, of tremendous benefit to western Canada. It provided for the equalization of rates between east and west. Prior to this, rates in the west were higher than those in the east. Rates have now been equalized under this section between east and west except for the unfinished business mentioned in the reports of the board which were tabled in the house and which anyone can see.
Then again, the legislation brought into effect the one and one-third rule which, as the committee knows, is of particular interest to the province of Alberta. The one and one-third rule is contained in section 337 of the Railway Act and it was, for so long as it was in operation, of great assistance to those who live in the intermediate territory. The one and one-third rule states that whenever any railway establishes a rate to Vancouver, say, it shall not charge more than one and one-third of that rate to intermediate points.
This, as I have said, was of great benefit to intermediate points until the judgment of the board of transport commissioners on agreed charges in the cast iron pipe case, interpreting section 32 of the Transport Act. This judgment nullified the benefits of the section inasmuch as the railways can contract themselves out of it by means of agreed charges. This is why the other evening I suggested to the house that consideration should be given to the effect of that section of the Railway Act, read in conjunction with section 32 of the Transport Act, to ascertain if it is not possible by some means or other to give the effect and benefit of the one and one-third rule to intermediate territory.
Another piece of legislation which was brought down was the provision for the uniform classification of systems of accounting for the railways. The house knows that for a long period there was tremendous difficulty between railways in Canada and in the United States because there was no uniform system of accounting, and the railways repeatedly asked parliament to institute a change and make accounting uniform. This was done by means of a section in the Railway Act. The interstate commerce commission of the United States had had such a unified system for many years. This was a good piece of legislation to be enacted, and it was one which

the provinces welcomed and which the provinces had been anxious to obtain.
Now I come to a point which will interest the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), dealing with competitive tariffs. At that time there was a great deal of complaint about the fact that the railways could simply file a competitive tariff. Well, the Railway Act was amended so that a competitive tariff filed with the board was subject to the same investigation and study as any other tariff. The board was enabled, because of that legislation, to go into that rate and ascertain whether or not it was compensatory to the railway. I believe, too, that it was of benefit to those who have to ship goods from one end of the country to the other.
Then there was a piece of legislation having to to with the recapitalization of the Canadian National Railways. As the house knows, the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act was introduced in this house. It changed 50 per cent of the company's interest bearing debt to preferred stock, on which after settling income taxes a dividend of 4 per cent would be paid from earnings. For a term of ten years, because of that legislation, until 1961, the railway is not required to pay interest on $100 million of its long term debt. The C.N.R. asked for this legislation and welcomed it, and I have no doubt that it assisted the railway a great deal.
We then brought in a bill to amend the Transport Act which provided for agreed charges for the Canadian National Railways and other lines. It, too, was of assistance to the railways.
In a word I repeat what I said earlier. All the recommendations made by the royal commission having to do with freight rates were implemented by the previous administration. The Prime Minister said the rates had gone up by 120 per cent. He did not say to what extent they had gone up in other countries, and neither did he include in the increase he mentioned that which has been made by the board of transport commissioners since the present government took office. There has been an additional 17 per cent increase, which brings the increase to 157 per cent rather than 120 per cent. The Prime Minister very carefully shied away from the 17 per cent increase which was put into effect by the board of transport commissioners under the regime of my hon. friends. If a comparison is made of increases in freight rates over the years from the time increases started after world war II, in 1948 let us say, up to the time the Prime Minister made his statement, it will be found that increases were greater 66968-9-151J

in the United States and as substantial, if not greater, in the United Kingdom.
There, sir, is the record in so far as the previous administration is concerned. There is a statement of what was done by the previous Liberal administration, what was done by the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues when they sat on the other side of the house to alleviate the burden of freight rates.
Let us see what was done by our hon. friends when they sat on this side of the chamber. This is important. Let us see how their conduct then compares with what it is today. Hon. gentlemen opposite when they sat on this side of the house sought to do away with the board of transport commissioners. They said the board was incompetent. They accused the board of being responsible for the increases in freight rates and for the state of confusion and chaos in which the country found itself in reference to the unfair application of freight rates. "It is not functioning as it should," said the opposition of that day. "The government," the opposition said, "should take over".
Do you know what they did then? They moved to reduce the estimates of the board of transport commissioners to $1. When I brought in my estimates on June 2, 1950 this was suggested by the then opposition. There will be found at page 3113 of Hansard of that date a record of the discussion wherein I made a lengthy statement about the position of freight rates as they were at that time. At the end of my speech the then leader of the opposition intervened in the debate, and at the conclusion of his remarks he moved that item No. 524, which provided for the salaries of the board of transport commissioners and the administration, maintenance and operation of the board in the amount of $624,800, be reduced to $1. That was the extent of the contribution of our hon. friends opposite when they sat on this side of the house. They would have put the board of transport commissioners out of operation.
Let us examine what they do now. Now that they are in office they renew and extend the terms of office of certain members of the board. I do not know how many have been extended, but I know the tenure of office of one or two has been extended. These are gentlemen for whom I have great regard and who have excellent records on the board. Now that hon. gentlemen opposite have the responsibility of office they renew and extend the terms of office of some men whom we appointed. But now here is the great joker of those who sit on the other side of the house. Do you know what they did in those days? They were against the establishment

of a royal commission. They said it would be a complete waste of time and would accomplish nothing. I am sorry the Prime Minister is not here because-

Yes, he may be. I regret that he is not here because I am sure he would enjoy my reading back to him some of the statements which were made during that debate. I remember the debate very well- oh, not the debate; the debates, because there were so many of them-and what was said particularly by hon. gentlemen opposite. Now we have the Prime Minister coming forth and saying he is going to establish a royal commission to deal with the transportation policy, the very thing hon. gentlemen opposite said would be utterly useless.
The then leader of the opposition made an interesting statement dealing with the appointment of a royal commission.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: What date was that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
January 14, 1949. It was quoted in the Montreal Star. The statement was made by the then leader of the opposition as he got off the train at Regina, and well do I remember it because I raised it in the house. This statement followed the announcement which had been made in the house by the former government to the effect that a royal commission would be established to deal with transportation policy and other matters. The press release reads:
The royal commission to investigate Canada's freight rate structure was tagged tonight (in Regina) by Hon. George Drew, Progressive Conservative leader, as a "waste of time." In a brief press conference on the second stop on his western tour, Mr. Drew said all essential data seemed to have been assembled and that the most important thing now was "determining the principle on which adjustment must be made of rates."
The then leader of the opposition thought a royal commission was a waste of time. Do you know what happened after that? The Conservative party held a convention here in Ottawa and passed a resolution stating that a royal commission would be a good thing. The resolution was to the effect that a royal commission should be established without delay to consider the whole transportation policy. They were running in both directions, their leader saying a royal commission was a waste of time and the party in convention saying they wanted a royal commission, just as they do now that they sit on the other side of the house. They run in two directions and sometimes in three, now that they sit where they do. We have had demonstrations of that

sort of thing on a number of occasions, as the house knows, and I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will not ask me to cite examples.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: The two royal commissions were for the purpose of determining different questions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
That is a very helpful
remark.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: It is true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
The other inconsistent attitude of our friends on the other side of the house had to do with horizontal rate increases. The house knows that once an increase in freight rates is granted, unfortunately, the effect is uniform. It is horizontal rate increase and it affects all parts of Canada detrimentally, but more particularly those parts in the east and in the west. According to our Conservative friends when they sat on this side of the house, the former government had done absolutely nothing to alleviate the burden of those uniform and horizontal freight rate increases and the former government should be condemned, the Prime Minister said. In fact in his statement in the house which I read earlier-and I shall repeat one sentence-he said, as reported at page 64 of Hansard:
We find ourselves, by horizontal increases, placed in an ever more difficult position.
Then again, during the election campaign the Prime Minister made some very pertinent statements about horizontal rate increases. Here is what he is reported to have said, according to a Canadian Press report published in the Windsor Daily Star of February 14, 1958:
On freight rates, Mr. Diefenbaker spelled out for the first time his government's apparent intention on the increase granted in January by the board of transport commissioners.
Listen to this:
"We said before we were in power that freight rates were unjustifiably high when raised horizontally.
Did we act? When the board allowed an increase, we held it up because it could not be justifiably brought into existence on the basis the increase was provided."
This statement was made on February 13, 1958. The effect of it is to say that horizontal increases are unjustifiably high and should not be allowed to go into effect. Well, what did the judgment of the board of transport commissioners say just a few months later? The board of transport commissioners, at page 14 of its judgment dated November 17, 1958, said this about horizontal rates:
There are many critics who point up the undesirability of horizontal increases, particularly stressing the amounts in cents per one hundred pounds by which such "spreads" increase, but it has not been shown in what way this feature can be avoided without either placing a higher rate

burden on short haul traffic or reducing the earning power of the carriers by granting them rate levels too low to produce the revenue they should be entitled to seek for the service they provide.
This is a complete answer to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: That is owing to competition, of course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: It does not matter what it is owing to. The point is that the Prime Minister and those who sat on this side of the house said they were going to remedy the impact and the effect of horizontal rates.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I think the point is that horizontal rates were increased over the years when the Liberals were in power, and that the amount of freight on which it was imposed was on a base of about 34 per cent. There was the difficulty over the horizontal rates, as my hon. friend knows; it was the application of the horizontal rates on such a narrow base.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I thank the minister for that intervention, and my reply to him is this. He has been in office now for 20 months. Here is the judgment of the board of transport commissioners which has increased freight rates by 17 per cent. The effect of that rate increase is uniform and horizontal; it applies all across Canada; it applies to the maritimes as it does to western Canada. It has done nothing to alleviate horizontal increases.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that the increase was 17 per cent. We have reduced it 7 per cent. Your party was in power for 23 years. Increases amounted to some 130 per cent, and your party did not reduce them 1 per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: The minister's party has increased it by 10 per cent. It went up 17 per cent and down 7 per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Ten per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I have no objection to my hon. friend interrupting my speech. As he knows, he has no right to interrupt or to inject a political note. But let me say this to him. The 17 per cent judgment is unjustified in so far as the attitude of our friends on the other side of the house is concerned because of the fact that the increase in the horizontal rates is definitely affected by the 17 per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: No, I will not allow the minister to interrupt me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Order. I am afraid the Chair cannot allow the house to anticipate the committee stage.
Freight Rates

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I have no objection to an interruption by the minister, but at least he should wait until I have replied to his statement. What I was saying is there has been a reduction of 7 per cent but there is still an increase of 10 per cent, and the effect on the horizontal and uniform rate increases is nonetheless 10 per cent in the maritime provinces, in the select territory where my hon. friend lives.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Put on by the board of transport commissioners.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I see; put on by the board of transport commissioners. But when my hon. friends were on this side of the house they said the board of transport commissioners were inadequate, were useless and were not doing the kind of job that should be done, and they made a motion to reduce the estimate to $1. I know my hon. friend does not like this; nonetheless I am trying to say that it is one thing to go out on the hustings and make a political speech and it is another thing to come into the house and give the facts as they should be given.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: You are making a political speech in the house and not on the hustings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Then my hon. friend can answer it. If I am making a political speech here my hon. friend can answer it, and I hope he will rise in his place and answer this. The statement I make now is that freight rates are far too important a matter to be dealt with politically.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
They should be dealt with by the board of transport commissioners. This is the board which has been maintained by parliament over the years to deal with this highly technical matter, and no political note should be injected in it. If my hon. friend believes that I am making a political speech now may I say that I would not have made it had the Prime Minister not made the statement the other day that while we were in office we had done absolutely nothing. I submit that we have done a great deal, and if my hon. friend who interrupts me now will consider the facts he will agree. He knows full well that the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which is of assistance to his part of the country, was passed by a Liberal administration. The increase of 10 per cent, from 20 per cent to 30 per cent, in traffic that moves, I believe, outside the select territory was also brought into effect by a Liberal administration. I am sure he will not deny that.
I have perhaps taken up too much time, sir. I did not intend to speak at this length, and I would not have risen in my place had

Freight Rates
those statements not been made by responsible members of the house here and outside the house on a matter which when I sat on the other side of the house I considered was a technical one to be dealt with by the board of transport commissioners, an expert body whose business, experience, duties and responsibilities are to fix, determine and enforce rates pursuant to section 328 of the Railway Act, as changing conditions from time to time require.
To sum up, I say that those who sit on the other side of the house, when they sat here, would do away with the board of transport commissioners, would call royal commissions useless and would remove the effect of horizontal freight rate increases. Now you are in office. Go ahead and remedy the impact of horizontal freight rate increases. Go ahead and do what the Turgeon royal commission, which conducted one of the best and most exhaustive studies ever made in this country, said could not be done with reference to horizontal increases except by the railways. In dealing with horizontal freight rate increases the commission had this to say:
The remedy does not lie in the prohibition, statutory or other, of horizontal increases, but is in the hands of the railways themselves. The railways should make studies of traffic conditions in all their bearings and should present to the board . . . proposals showing not only their maximum percentage increase requirement, but also, among other particulars, varying percentage increases on different commodities, flat, instead of percentage increases when these are more suitable, and maxima in appropriate cases in cents per 10O pounds or other unit.
The recommendation by the board of transport commissioners with reference to horizontal increases was that no legislative amendment was required, that the Railway Act in its present form was sufficient and authorized the railways and the board to deal with this problem satisfactorily. But you on the other side of the house have said, "Oh no, wait a minute; we shall deal with this and wiR remedy the impact when we get into office". I have referred to two statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), one made in Saskatoon and the other made in the house. If he can do it I will be the first to commend him because I know the people of Canada will welcome anything that will have the effect of alleviating the burden of horizontal increases in the freight rate structure.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that the freight rate situation is satisfactory?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I certainly have not said that.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: He says that nothing can be done, according to the Turgeon report.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I said no such thing.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: You implied that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: If I implied that, then I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I was dealing with horizontal increases when I made the statement I did and I was not dealing with the whole freight rate structure. Of course the freight rate structure can be bettered. That is the object of P.C.1487, to equalize freight rates all across Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: That is the object of this government to better the freight rate structure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
I hope the government will be successful. What I was dealing with when my hon. friend interrupted me was only a small fraction of the structure, namely horizontal and uniform rate increases, and the board in its last judgment says it has not been shown in what way this can be done; that the railways are the ones to alleviate horizontal increases. When I was dealing with horizontal increases I was simply replying to statements that had been made earlier by those on the other side of the house.
So that there may be no doubt in the minds of hon. members let me say that of course there remains a great deal to do. There are still inequities, there is still discrimination, there is still equalization that needs to be brought about with reference to the freight rate structure, there is still need of a national transportation policy for Canada. I presume that will be the object of the royal commission. I presume that will be one of the terms of reference of the commission. I do not pretend that the situation is fine in the finest of worlds. What I am saying is that we have done a great deal to alleviate the effect and burden of discrimination, inequalities and inequities in the freight rate structure, and I think I have put enough evidence on the recoid to indicate to our friends on the other side that while we were in office we did not simply do nothing as our hon. friends try to indicate.
I have been much too long, Mr. Speaker, and I simply want to conclude by saying that with respect to any measures the government brings before us, either through this subsidy which we will support and try to strengthen when the bill goes to the committee or through the scope, broad as it may be, of a royal commission, we will support the government because having in mind the tremendous distances over which freight has to move to the extremities of our country it becomes more and more important to remove these inequities. The former administration

removed a large portion of them and should be given credit instead of criticism.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak for a few minutes on the bill which, from the point of view of members of this group, is a measure of expediency to meet a long term and continuing problem that is of concern to large sections of the Canadian people. It simply reduces from 17 per cent to 10 per cent the increase in freight rates which the people have to pay at the present time. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that during the exchange between the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) and the former minister of transport with respect to what the present government had done in 20 months compared with what the former government had done in 22 years I made a quick calculation, and if my calculation is correct the average rate of freight rate increase per year during the former government's term of office was slightly under five per cent while, allowing for the $20 million subsidy, the average rate of increase in freight rates during the last 20 months has been something slightly over six per cent. There is not a great deal of difference with respect-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Hardly a logical conclusion.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
-to whether one government or the other was in power. I wish to present the representations of this group regarding this very serious and complicated question. I might say it is not a subject on which I enjoy speaking because I admit quite frankly I can no more explain the idiosyncrasies of the freight rate structure than fly but we do have certain opinions with respect to how freight charges are arrived at, the effect that increases in freight rates have and the attitude of the Canadian people.
The representations of our group are based on a knowledge of the seriousness of this continuing situation as indicated by the repeated protests year after year made against increases in freight rates by provincial governments, farmers' organizations, the British Columbia fruit growers' association and organizations representing lumber manufacturers, mining and other industries. The representations of the farmers' organizations have been placed before the house a number of times by other members of this group and I am not going to deal with them further. But I do want to say a few words with respect to the tree fruit industry, the lumber industry and the mining industry.
The tree fruit industry of British Columbia, with which I am particularly well acquainted, has made submissions to hearings of the board of transport commissioners on
Freight Rates
several occasions vigorously opposing increases in freight tariffs. They have done so because they have done everything possible to lower costs by improving packaging and extending markets with an aggressive sales policy. In other words, they have done all they can to help themselves. Regardless of every effort in this respect the industry is having a very difficult time indeed. Even at present the growers are receiving little more and in many cases less than the cost of production. 1 am sure a good number of members recall that in 1955 the cost of production of apples in British Columbia was approximately $2.50 a box and the average return to the fruit growers of British Columbia for all grades was about 72 cents a box. That gives one some idea of why they are so concerned about the cost of transportation for their commodity.
Again, what about the lumber industry? I am very well acquainted with a wide section of the lumber industry and it too has suffered very seriously in the last 12 or 18 months from lack of markets and low prices. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, in the last 15 months a good number of small saw mills in British Columbia have been obliged to close down because they could not continue to operate or could not continue to make a profit that made it possible for them to operate. Others have continued to operate under great difficulties and in most cases up until quite recently on an extremely narrow margin. The industry in British Columbia has made repeated representations to the board of transport commissioners and to the cabinet committee on freight rates because of the seriousness of the cost of transportation to this industry. I am sure the minister realizes what it means to these smaller mills, particularly in the mountainous sections of British Columbia, to have even this ten per cent increase in freight rates at this time.
Then I am sure all of us know the difficulties that have been experienced by quite wide sections of the mining industry which have suffered a decline in the price of base metals in the last two years particularly. Here again in this connection may I say that in my constituency and in surrounding constituencies a number of small properties have been obliged to close down, to a large extent because of the cost of transportation of their product to the markets concerned. These transportation costs are a most important factor particularly with respect to the smaller segments of the lumber industry and the mining industry and in connection with farming and fruit farming in general.
For a few moments I want to deal with our two arguments-we have stated them before

Freight Rates
but on this motion for second reading we wish to repeat them-against the position taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company when seeking increased freight rates. I might say that my reading of the record in years past would indicate that the whole pattern of freight rates in Canada seems to be established by the attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. We in this group believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company suffers from two diseases, namely economic schizophrenia and income tax anaemia. That is our approach to the position of the C.P.R. We believe both of these diseases can be cured by a shot of government action and we believe it is about time that something was done in that respect.
We think the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has what we would term a split personality. The company has for years assiduously developed the legend that its corporate assets are arbitrarily divisible as between the rail and non-rail operations. The company's entire case, as far as we can see, rests on the assumption that its railway operations can be divorced from the other lucrative enterprises which account for such a large part of its income. In our opinion, this is a completely unsound and unethical position. For instance, when a shareholder purchases stock in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company he does not buy shares reflecting the assets of the railway as distinct from the non-operating assets but purchases shares that reflect the earnings of the total assets of the company. Why should not the company's rates, taxes and charges be assumed to be on the same basis?
I want to quote briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 19, 1957. It was written by a gentleman who is designated as "S.M.". I think this editorial clearly states the case and I am going to quote it in full because I think it is worthy of being on the record. It states the case much better than I could do it of my own volition and it presents our argument in this respect. The editorial is headed "C.P.R.'s Claim Challenged". This was one of a series of articles dealing with proposed freight rate increases. It reads as follows:
Ottawa: The Canadian Pacific Railway Company for years has assiduously developed a legend that its corporate assets are arbitrarily divisible as between rail and non-rail operations.
Every application for higher freight rates depends upon this supposition, and none more than the case currently being considered by the transport board. The C.P.R. has asked the board to accept as a rate base the sum of $1,146 millions, which the company says is its net investment in railway property.
The C.P.R.'s entire case rests on the assumption that its railway operations can be arbitrarily divorced from those other lucrative enterprises which account for such a large part of its income.

The validity of this argument has been directly challenged by a paper prepared for the board by Prof. Vernon Fowke of the University of Saskatchewan. Prof. Fowke's study clearly demonstrates that neither parliament nor the original officers of the company intended that these ancillary operations should be anything but part of the company's general transportation system.
The Canadian Pacific Railway Act of 1881 defines the purposes of the company: To construct a rail link to the Pacific coast, to buy or build a line to the Atlantic, to acquire such other facilities as would contribute to a well-rounded transportation system, and to operate the whole in perpetuity.
The charter was amended in 1902 to broaden this scope by including such non-rail operations as mining and smelting,-
I may say that includes an extremely profitable mining and smelting company which last year declared a profit of over $14 million.
-irrigation, generation of electricity and iron, steel and lumber manufacturing.
The 1902 amendments specified that these powers were to be exercised "for the purposes of the company," and this phrase or its equivalent is contained in each amending clause. Its inclusion, as Prof. Fowke observes, is no mere legal verbiage, for parliament in 1881 had clearly defined these purposes as the operation of the railway.
Any recent annual report of the C.P.R. will illustrate how far the company has departed from these purposes. Its "other income" in 1951 was nearly $30 millions, not a penny of which was credited to rail operations.
"The wording of the various sections of the (1902) statute makes it abundantly clear," Prof. Fowke states, "that the parliament of Canada had no intention that the beneficiary of the statute, the C.P.R., might henceforth or at any time exercise its additional powers as ends in themselves or for purposes divorced in any way from the purposes for which the company was originally formed."
Parliament clearly had not contemplated a company which would pour its railway profits into vast non-rail operations, at the same time charging the public with the entire cost, including corporate income taxes, of running the railway alone.
Nor had parliament ever intended that the 25 million acres in land and $25 millions in subsidies which it granted the C.P.R. would be used, not for the benefit of its customers, but for the greater reward of its shareholders.
The 1902 powers, the subsidies and the land grants were given, Prof. Fowke says, to assist the C.P.R. in the fulfilment of its purposes as an instrument of national policy, the central object of which remained that of operating a railway.
I quoted that editorial in full, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is an excellent exposition of the facts of the situation as we see it with respect to the C.P.R.'s continued insistence on divorcing its railway operations from its other much more profitable operations.
I now come to the question of what I term the income tax anaemia; that is, the method by which the company under the income tax provisions of legislation makes annual additions to the so-called tax equalization reserve, whereby they make provision

for modernization, dieselization, improvement in track and so on. It is an extremely complicated question indeed. For the sake of exactitude I just want to quote briefly from one or two briefs that were presented to the board of transport commissioners by various transport officials who make a specialty of this subject. In that connection I will quote first of all from page 2 of a report by the national association of railroad and utilities commissioners, 1955, report of committee on depreciation. I quote this one paragraph because it illustrates what is happening at the present time under the present income tax policy pursued by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. At page 2 of the report we find this:
Heretofore, public utilities generally have employed the straight line method of computing depreciation expense for income tax purposes. For many years, prior to about 15 years ago, electric and gas utilities computed depreciation expense for income tax purposes according to the straight line method but employed other methods for corporate accounting purposes. To a limited extent this is still true. In general, those utilities claimed and were allowed more depreciation expense in their tax returns than they recorded in their corporate books of account. A study by the securities and exchange commission for the ten-year period, 1930-39, disclosed that 168 electric and gas utilities charged 53.64 per cent more depreciation for tax purposes than they recorded in their corporate accounts. The higher allowances for depreciation expense resulted in consequential tax savings as compared to the taxes which would have been terrible had the allowance for depreciation been equal to that recorded on the books.
That is exactly the same principle which has been given effect at the present time by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and to which we object.
Then there were further representations made before the committee. I think they were presented by the gentlemen representing the province of British Columbia in this particular case. I would like to read from appendix A of the report from the committee on accounts and statistics, which is a report dealing with the accounting treatment of tax reduction occasioned by depreciation provisions of the internal revenue code of 1954. They used this to illustrate this practice which has been transferred from the United States to Canada in recent years. This is what is said on page 12 of this appendix:
It should be clear from the foregoing evidence that the new methods of accelerated depreciation authorized in the internal revenue code of 1954, and particularly the years-digits method, offer management the opportunity to make considerably increased annual depreciation charges for an indefinite period and, consequently, very great tax savings. Moreover, contrary to erroneous general belief, these tax savings will be permanent-at least as long as the law remains in effect. In no legitimate sense may they be considered tax deferrals.
Freight Rates
Then on page 13 I read the following with respect to this problem:
The committee is convinced that the use of the liberalized depreciation procedures permitted by the 1954 revenue act results in tax reduction, not tax deferral, and that it would be contrary to sound accounting principles and to the provisions of the uniform systems of accounts to record such tax reduction in a deferred credit account.
The real regulatory problem in connection with tax reduction arising through liberalized depreciation is how to treat the tax reduction in fixing rates for service. This of course is not an accounting matter; however, the committee does have some thoughts on this question and believes the following suggestions are worthy of consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I have just dealt briefly with two aspects of the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the first of insisting on separating its railway assets from its other much more profitable assets when considering the cost of operating the railway, and the need according to the company for increased freight rates and, second, the annual addition to the so-called tax equalization reserve fund.
We in this group believe that a national transportation policy that co-ordinates air, land and water transportation in Canada is urgently required. We think we require a policy in which consideration will be given to the needs of every section of Canada as to how this country can most economically and effectively be given the service, both freight and passenger, to meet its requirements. We believe this national transportation policy should make provision for an efficient service to all portions of Canada, and should make provision for the equalization of freight rates and the necessary standards of passenger service to all parts of the country. In our opinion the terms of reference of the royal commission should provide for a thorough study of all aspects of the transportation problem as a basis for the planning of a national transportation policy by this House of Commons and this government. Until we approach this problem in an over-all way we are simply going to continue this "bits and bobs" policy year after year, with the companies asking for an increase in freight rates, farmers' organizations, mining and lumbering industries appealing against the increases, and then some temporary expedient being brought before this house to meet the situation and soft soap over it temporarily, just as we are doing in this bill, thus getting no further toward a real solution of the question. Under present circumstances agricultural, lumbering, mining and other industries suffer from an inequitable freight rate structure. Also many Canadians suffer from the discontinuance of branch line passenger services,

Freight Rates
which in some cases should not and would not be discontinued if this government governed Canada in these cases rather than let the wishes of the C.P.R. prevail.
Mr. Speaker, once again I cannot resist bringing to the attention of the house one situation just to illustrate the effect of this "bits and bobs" policy and the fact that what Mr. Crump says goes, rather than what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) says, with respect to meeting the needs of various sections of Canada. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, that under present circumstances our Minister of Transport in effect has to go cap in hand almost on bended knee to ask Mr. Crump if he would do something to correct an injustice which exists with respect to transportation services provided in some parts of Canada. That is what is actually happening at the present time, and in the opinion of the members of this group it is an outrageous situation which we are going to continue to protest against until we get some remedy. I cannot believe that this government is going to allow this situation to continue. As I said before, I cannot resist bringing to the attention of the house again the fact that in southeastern British Columbia, where 135,000 people produce between $200 million and $250 million worth of mineral, forest and agricultural products, they have to suffer a Budd car service from Vancouver to Lethbridge where the young and the aged, the decrepit, lame, invalid and sick are required to sit up for 24 hours and subsist on dry sandwiches and cool coffee. There is a direct illustration of what happens with respect to this "bits and bobs" policy. This is the passenger service which is being provided by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the southeastern portion of British Columbia, and regardless of how much the Minister of Transport tries to help us, and I know he has done his very best, still Mr. Crump says nothing doing. He says what is going to be done or not done.
We submit that that situation should be remedied, and we will continue to squawk until it is, even though I find that because of my continued reference to this injustice some of my lady friends around the building are now referring to me as "The Kettle Valley Kid". It is about time the government of Canada demonstrated that it meant to govern with respect to a national transportation policy for this country. Members of this group trust that this is the last time that this house will be required to deal with this problem on a temporary, piecemeal, titbits basis, and hope that a national transportation policy will result from the royal commission's recommendations, which we trust will be within a year, and that consequent action will be taken

on the part of this government, which has promised so much and to date done so little to meet this problem.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has just made an admirable speech except that his last words should have been "promised so much and have done so much". Coming from British Columbia, I would not expect the hon. member to have anything but the highest praise for this government, which is the first government to have recognized the peculiar problems existing in the extremities of the country.
I was very interested to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who spent 90 per cent of his time castigating the government and the last 10 per cent telling us what a fine bill this was, what a lot it would do for the country and what a lot there was still to do in the way of equalizing freight rates.
With regard to British Columbia, I should like to quote from a brief prepared by the British Columbia lumber manufacturers association which stated that since April, 1948 seven freight rate increases had been approved by the board of transport commissioners and that the total cumulative increase had been 125 per cent up to the beginning of 1958. This included the 3J per cent which this government disallowed in its first term of office, and all hon. members from British Columbia know how widely and heartily the government was praised in the press of the province for this decision. In circumstances with which all hon. members are familiar, the government was faced with a 17 per cent increase in freight rates, an increase which had to come about if we were to keep our railways in a position to serve this country and provide the essential transport facilities which a modern society needs. So what has the government done? It has brought in, not bits and pieces of legislation, but an idea in legislation which is new. I wish the hon. member for Laurier would listen to this: for 22 years during which his party governed this country there was nothing new in the way this legislation is new, because this legislation recognizes the needs and extremities of transport users in this country.
The effect of succeeding increases in freight rates had been to increase the cost of shipping a thousand board feet of lumber from Vancouver to Winnipeg from $14.70 prior to April 8, 1948 to $34.60 by January 1, 1957. On the same basis, shipments to Toronto increased in cost from $22 to $40.30. Because of these increases there set in a progressive decline in shipments of coast lumber to the eastern Canadian markets, a decline of some

47 per cent from almost 10,000 carloads in 1948 to 5,290 carloads in 1957. As every hon. member from British Columbia knows, or ought to know, our prosperity is dependent entirely on the prosperity of the woods industry, because at least 25 per cent of our payroll comes from forest industries, and as forest industries go, so goes British Columbia.
I have just finished checking with the board, as far as I can, with regard to the latest increase-the increase of 17 per cent- and I think it would be of interest to hon. members to know that rates on traffic originating in British Columbia on the coast and in the interior would have had to bear that 17 per cent increase almost in its entirety and, in consequence those shippers and those producers who are dependent upon the movement of the products they have produced will gain the greatest benefit from the present legislation since, as I have said, this measure has been tailored to help the maritimes and the far west. Further, as I also said, this is the first time anything has been done in this house to help, particularly, the province from which I come.
The hon. member for Laurier mentioned the Turgeon royal commission and the bridge subsidy on traffic across the northern shores of lake Superior, and mentioned what important aid this provided in marrying the two sections of Canada. The bridge subsidy is a very fine thing, but there are other non-productive areas in Canada; one might call the trackage through the mountains a non-productive area. But what has been the effect of the bridge subsidy? It has certainly been good, but it was not tailored to suit our needs, because the effect of the subsidy, having regard to the location of the bridge, has been to increase our cost of shipping into our legitimate markets, that is, the prairie provinces, in relation to the cost of eastern manufacturers shipping to the same region. This has come about because of the location of that bridge.
The fact that an artificially low rate is in existence across this trackage creates a subsidy which helps in shipping west, and which does help the west to ship to the east when shipments are being made east of the bridge but not when they are being made to points west of the bridge. So although this has helped us to a limited degree it will not do so to anything like the same extent as this measure will do.
To give hon. members some idea of the difference in the application of these rates I should like to point out that the 161 per cent freight rate increase granted in 1953 resulted in an increase in gross railway revenue of only 2.8 per cent. Why was
Freight Rates
this? It was because much of the traffic, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, would have been diverted to other means of transportation had the rates been so increased. The rates were, therefore, held down to the competitive rates in those areas, but where the traffic would bear the increase, that is where the increase was placed and this was, of course, in those areas where a widely-flung trucking system does not exist and where there are no facilities for water travel such as exist in Ontario and Quebec. Incidentally this substantial increase of 161 per cent was not mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier. With regard to this increase, his government simply said: there it is, let us put it through.
This measure which we are debating today is one which will provide us with immediate help. We are not being asked to wait for the length of time it would take to receive a report from a royal commission. This is something which will be of help right away, immediate assistance such as has been noticed in field after field of government endeavour.
The hon. member for Laurier made great play with the mountain differential and the fact that the one and a half rule as against the 50 per cent premium for transportation through the mountains was cut to one and a quarter and then to one. They recognize he said, that there was no real justice in this differential, and I suggest that that was about the only thing they ever did to help the province of British Columbia. This legislation is legislation tailored to help us in the west and to help our brothers in the maritimes in the most practical and common-sense fashion.
I think when the time comes for the proposed commission to investigate the entire freight rate structure, close attention should be given to the simplification of that structure, because it needs amendment and needs to be drawn in such a way that rates are truly equalized-so that when a manufacturer in British Columbia is shipping, say, to Brandon he will pay the same rate per ton per mile as a manufacturer in Montreal would have to pay. When such a situation as this comes about we shall, indeed, have equality of competition and we in the west will be able to share equally with the eastern manufacturers in access to Canadian markets.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house any longer, but I would say, in conclusion, that this is one of the most progressive steps as far as the west is concerned, and one of the best steps as far as British Columbia is concerned, that this government has taken to date, and I commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) for having

Freight Rates
introduced this bill and suggest it should be made law as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister is listening to what is being said by those who are speaking in support of this bill. A few moments ago I thought he was showing a degree of discourtesy in not listening with bated breath to the fine speech that was being made.
The thing that concerns me in relation to this bill being sent to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is this. What is going to happen in the committee? What information are we going to get with which to operate in terms of an explanation as to how this act is to work? I have just been looking at the bill again and clause 7 continues to confuse me. I think the minister has not given us a sufficiently lucid explanation of what is meant by that provision and perhaps he will do so later.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) gave some specific instances of how our particular region in northwestern Ontario suffers with respect to inequalities as far as freight rates are concerned and I commend his remarks to the minister's attention. An hon. gentleman from the west coast who spoke earlier this afternoon remarked on the bridge territory on which there is a $7 million subsidy. There are some points I wish to reinforce and underscore in this regard. In many ways the bridge is the greatest weakness in the whole freight rate structure in Canada. Every argument put forward by the western provinces commences with a reference to the bridge and the fact that it is not economical because not enough traffic originates from the bridge.
One reason why the people in northwestern Ontario are sceptical about the vision, and you cannot blame them for it, is because they live in a part of the country in which they would like to see displayed much more evidence of vision so far as providing industry and revenue are concerned. In no area would this be more effective than in the field of railway development. If we could get more internal traffic development, especially on the Canadian National Railways, such as we have at Steep Rock and Manitouwadge, perhaps the basic problem of the railway structure will ultimately be cleared up.
When this bill is before the Committee I hope we will have some explanation of the bridge subsidy. It was set at $7 million, approximately seven years ago I believe. In view of the upward trends in cost that we have experienced why has not the bridge subsidy gone up? When the bill goes before the

committee we should get an interrelated picture of all aspects of the freight rate situation. I remarked the other day that we members of parliament are amateurs, duds and boobs with respect to this field which is one of the most difficult to understand and appreciate. When the minister appears before that committee I suggest he have with him departmental experts and advisers from the board of transport commissioners. They should be there throughout the time the committee is sitting so they would be on call to guide us as we move through consideration of the bill. It is important that we understand this legislation even though it is an interim measure because after a year there will be the report of the royal commission to consider.
The bridge territory in which my constituency lies is one of the fundamental regions at which we must look. We have been told by experts that the highest freight rates in Canada obtain in the area. That is an important internal concern. As a national problem, if we do not get more traffic originating in the bridge area, the discrepancies and the problem of equalization will continue to exist and may exist for a long time.
These remarks lead us into a reference of the vision, of course. Northwestern Ontario is a vast area approximately 600 or 700 miles in breadth and depth. The whole area of the maritimes and part of British Columbia could be tucked into this portion of the country, it is that large. I would suggest to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that it concentrate on a development policy for this area which would do a lot for the freight rate situation.
I hope the minister will give us a nice, slow, amiable run-down on where he stands in relation to the bill, that the bill will be sent to the committee and that the committee will do a good job.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up too much time of the house on this subject because no doubt there are many other hon. members who wish to participate in the discussion. I do believe, however, it is my duty to bring to the attention of the house some facts about the situation in regard to freight rates as they apply in the northern part of Manitoba. It is my belief that the people in that area suffer very greatly under some of the highest freight rates that exist in this country.
I wish to refer briefly to an article which appeared in the November 11, 1958, issue of The Rural Co-Operator published by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture in Toronto.

In an article entitled, "Competition Myth Costs Money", the following appears:
What Canada has, in effect, is a giant railway monopoly half owned by the public (C.N.R.) and half owned by private business (C.P.R.). We pay for the duplication of overhead but receive none of the advantages of competition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in many areas of Canada that would be a ridiculous statement, as you no doubt realize that many areas benefit to a marked degree from competitive rates. If people in those areas were to compare the rates of which they may take advantage with those that exist in the area I represent they would see the situation in its true light.
We have only one railway in northern Manitoba and at many points no highway parallels this railway. The rates are high on most goods and materials that come into the area and of course the working man is the one who pays the shot.
There is one aspect of this problem which is difficult to understand. In places like Lynn Lake and other points along the Hudson bay line where there are no highways, families who wish to go out on an annual holiday are required to ship their automobiles to the nearest highway by rail. There is a loading charge for putting the automobile in the box car, a high transportation cost for bringing it out to the highway and an unloading charge and on the return trip the same charges are applicable. Those charges although high are probably justified but one thing that should be examined is this. When two families are bringing out their cars there is no reduction in price and both pay the rates applicable to the shipment of a single vehicle.
There are many other examples that could be cited of situations of this kind existing in the area of northern Manitoba. Additional freight rates apply on goods going north of The Pas on the Hudson bay line. I suppose this is also a result of lack of competition, but these things should be inquired into.
I might refer also to the situation which I believe points up the necessity of a very full investigation into this matter. I would like to refer to the Arthur D. Little Incorporated report, which was an economic survey of northern Manitoba. In this report, which has just recently been released, transportation is mentioned. The report says:
Transportation is of considerable importance in pulp and paper operations, both for the supply of raw materials and for the delivery of finished products. For raw material supply, northern Manitoba offers facilities comparable with areas in which pulp and paper mills have been successfully established:	for the delivery of finished
products, however, it suffers from a serious competitive freight rate disadvantage.
The report goes on to deal with transportation to markets and it says:
Freight Rates
Rates that have been quoted by the Canadian National Railways for newsprint from a point (Pit Siding) near the Kelsey power plant would have the effect of virtually excluding shipments to Canadian markets. Rates to United States destinations, however, are by no means unsatisfactory.
These remarks are made in relation to a survey which was made by Arthur D. Little Incorporated in respect to the possibilities of opening up a pulp and paper mill in this area where, I might say, an industry of this kind is very badly needed.
I should like to give a comparison of those rates further to bring out the point that a full investigation into this matter should be undertaken soon. The freight rates which were quoted to ship newsprint from this area were from Pit Siding to Saskatoon, a distance of 560 miles. The rate per ton quoted was $28.4. To Winnipeg, a distance of 724 miles, the comparative rate was $34 per ton. To Fort William, a distance of 1,157 miles, the rate per ton was $48.6.
I should like to give a further comparison to show why I think an investigation of our freight rate set up is very necessary. To ship the same newsprint from Pit Siding to Minneapolis, a distance of 1,141 miles, would cost $17.80 per ton; to ship it to Milwaukee, a distance of 1,456 miles, would cost $22 per ton; and to ship it to Chicago, a distance of 1,535 miles, the rate is $22 per ton. Apparently we are permitted to ship newsprint from Pit Siding to Chicago, a distance of 1,535 miles, for $22 a ton and yet to ship it within Canada to Fort William, 1,157 miles, almost 400 miles fewer than to Chicago, the rate is $48.6 a ton, more than double. I realize Mr. Speaker, that I am certainly by no means an authority on freight rates, especially rates of this nature. In fact, I have a very limited knowledge of them. No doubt in those comparisons of shipping within Canada and to the United States there is something which comes under our export regulations. However, I do think that since the northern areas are so badly in need of industry, these things should be investigated as quickly as possible.
I notice that the explanatory note of the bill we are discussing reads:
The purpose of this bill is to provide for the revision of certain class and commodity freight rates and to compensate the companies to the extent of $20 million.
I sincerely hope that some of this $20 million will be used to lessen the burden on the people of those outlying areas who are paying tremendous freight rates at the present time.
